note.title: Read Names, Colours and Numbers
note.summary: Read about Mei and Ravi sharing things at school.
body: Listen to one sentence at a time. Find the name of the child, then point to the object that the child has.
A colour word tells us more about an object. In “a red book”, red tells us the colour of the book.
A number word tells us how many. Read “two blue pencils” slowly, and show two fingers as you say two.

vocabulary.meaning: Let someone else use something too.

note.title: Follow People and Places
note.summary: Follow a lost pencil in a school reading corner.
body: Names help you follow a story. When a sentence uses “he” or “she”, read the sentence before it to find the person. Keep track of what each child does as the story moves on.
Place words show where something is. “Under” means below an object, while “beside” means next to it. Read the whole sentence so you know which object the place word describes.
A story may give a reason using “so”. Read what happens before and after this word. This helps you connect an action with its purpose, such as moving something so another person can find it.
keyPoints: Match each action with a name.
Use place words to find objects.

note.title: Read Events in Order
note.summary: Read how two classmates choose leaves for a display in Ipoh.
body: Sequence words help you follow events. “First” starts a set of actions, “next” introduces another action, and “finally” shows the last one. Use these words when you retell a story.
Characters can notice different things about the same object. Read what each person says or does before deciding what they think. A changed plan can make an ordinary event interesting.
To answer a question about a reason, look for “because” and read the words that follow it. Choose the reason stated in the story instead of adding a reason from your own experience.
keyPoints: Find the stated reason for a choice.

vocabulary.meaning: Objects arranged for people to look at.
An arrangement of shapes or marks.

reading.title: The Leaf We Kept
reading.summary: Read how two classmates choose leaves for a display in Ipoh.
body: On Saturday, Nisha and Hakim visited their neighbourhood hall in Ipoh. Their class was making a leaf display. They brought fallen leaves from their gardens in a basket.
First, they spread the leaves on a table. Nisha noticed that one leaf was torn. Hakim wanted to leave it out, but Nisha kept it because its tiny holes looked like a pattern.

Next, they drew the leaves in a notebook and wrote their colours below the drawings. Finally, they showed the display to their teacher. She asked about the torn leaf. Nisha smiled and explained her choice.

note.title: Connect a Problem with Its Solution
note.summary: Find out how a trial helps pupils improve an open-day reading table.
body: A story about solving a problem often includes a first plan, a difficulty and a revised plan. Notice what the characters discover during a trial. This helps explain why their arrangement changes.

Comparisons need a clear feature. Something may be easier to see without being larger or newer. Look for the feature the passage describes, such as the position of a sign or the visibility of a cover.
A useful solution can meet two needs at once. When answering, check that your option keeps both needs. Use the reported result of the trial as evidence that the new plan worked in this situation.
keyPoints: Identify the difficulty in the first plan.
Compare the feature named in the passage.
Check how the solution meets both needs.

vocabulary.meaning: A test to see how something works.

reading.title: A Better Reading Table
reading.summary: Find out how a trial helps pupils improve an open-day reading table.
body: The pupils at a school in Kuching were preparing a quiet reading table for open day. Farah placed six books in a deep basket. Daniel made a sign saying, “Choose a story and return it here.” They expected younger children to visit with their families.

During a trial, Daniel’s little brother could read the sign but could not see the books at the bottom of the basket. Farah suggested putting the books flat on the table. Daniel worried that this would cover the sign.

They tried a second arrangement. Farah stood the sign behind the basket and put three books on the table, leaving three inside. Now the visitor could see some covers and still read the instructions. He chose a story about a fish. The pupils kept this arrangement because both the books and the sign were easy to see.

note.title: Use Dialogue to Explain a Change
note.summary: Explore how feedback changes the labels at a class book exchange.
body: Dialogue reveals a character’s response to an event. Read the speaker’s exact concern before explaining a change of plan. One person’s comment supports a conclusion about that person, not automatically about everyone.

Look for a contrast between the first attempt and the revised version. Ask what each version describes and what information it gives. A practical revision often changes the feature that caused the original difficulty.

Support an interpretation with an action or quotation from the story. For example, a character’s later choice may show how a revised plan helps. Keep your explanation close to that evidence and avoid inventing feelings.
keyPoints: Use a speaker’s words to explain a concern.
Compare the first and revised plans.
Support an interpretation with a specific detail.

vocabulary.meaning: An event where people give something and receive something else.
A person’s skill at doing something.

reading.title: Labels That Invite Readers
reading.summary: Explore how feedback changes the labels at a class book exchange.
body: When a class in Penang organised a book exchange, Aina volunteered to write the labels. Each pupil could bring one book and choose another. The organisers wanted everyone to find a story they would enjoy, even if they did not know its title.

At first, Aina labelled the baskets “Easy” and “Difficult”. Her friend Vikram hesitated beside a basket. “I like short stories, but I do not like choosing a basket that calls my reading easy,” he said quietly. Aina realised that her labels described readers’ ability more than the stories themselves.

She asked the group to suggest labels about the books. They chose “Animals”, “Adventures” and “Everyday Life”. Aina also added a short note to each book, giving its page count and saying whether it had pictures. These details helped pupils judge the length without ranking their ability.

When the exchange opened, Vikram picked an animal story with many pictures. Aina asked if the new system helped. “Yes,” he said. “Now I can start with what interests me.” She decided to keep the topic labels for the next exchange.

note.title: Judge a Plan Using Limited Evidence
note.summary: Use a small trial and visitor choices to evaluate a reading-event plan.
body: When characters disagree about a plan, identify the purpose behind each suggestion. Then follow how a trial gives them information. Evidence from a small trial can guide a decision without settling every future question.

Distinguish an observation from an interpretation. “Two children wanted to exchange their books” reports what happened. “The same pack will not suit everyone” interprets that observation. Check that the interpretation stays within the evidence.

A careful conclusion names its limits. A plan that works for one group on one afternoon may need another check in a different setting. Look for phrases that tell you whose experience the claim covers and when it applies.
keyPoints: Identify what the trial is meant to discover.
Connect the revised plan with observed choices.
Keep conclusions within the group and event studied.

vocabulary.meaning: Information used to support a conclusion.
Able to change to meet different needs.

reading.title: The Story-Pack Trial
reading.summary: Use a small trial and visitor choices to evaluate a reading-event plan.
body: For a neighbourhood reading afternoon in Johor Bahru, Liyana’s class prepared story packs for younger children. Each pack contained a book, a pencil and a card for drawing a favourite scene. The class had enough materials for twenty packs, but nobody knew how many families would attend.

Amir suggested making all twenty packs immediately. Liyana preferred to assemble ten and keep the remaining materials separate. If visitors wanted different books, the pupils could offer a choice instead of opening finished packs. Their teacher asked them to test the idea with three families before deciding.

During the trial, two children wanted to exchange the books in their packs. Another child wanted only a book because she had brought her own drawing materials. The families liked the activity, but their choices showed that identical packs would not suit everyone.

The class set up three baskets: one for books, one for pencils and one for drawing cards. A volunteer explained that children could take the materials they needed. Amir recorded what visitors chose so the class would have evidence for planning another event.

By the end of the afternoon, eighteen books had been chosen, along with twelve pencils and fifteen cards. Liyana did not call the trial proof that every future event should use baskets. She said it showed that flexible choices had worked for this group, on this afternoon.
